name: Tilleul de Châteauvieux

location.address: Place de la Chapelle de Château-Vieux, hameau de Châteauvieux, 74500 Féternes, Haute-Savoie
location.neighbourhood: Châteauvieux hamlet, 1.5 km west of Féternes centre

access: Free. Stands on the public square beside the 13th-century Chapelle de Château-Vieux, and is the named stop on a signposted local walking loop ("Boucle du tilleul et de la pierre à cupules à Féternes", per lofficiel.net and the Pays d'Evian tourist office cc-peva.fr, which references a downloadable "Sentier du Tilleul" trail leaflet). No gate, no ticket.
transport: Rural hamlet with no rail/transit stop; reached by road from Féternes centre (about 1.5km) or Thonon-les-Bains further out. Walking or driving only, no public transport.
story:
This lime measures 10.2 metres around the trunk at chest height. Two separate surveys came back with 10.18 and 10.2, which is about as close to agreement as tape measures around an old lime ever get.

It stands on the square beside the Chapelle de Château-Vieux, a thirteenth-century chapel in a hamlet a kilometre and a half west of Féternes, in the hills above Lac Léman. The A.R.B.R.E.S. association labelled it a Remarkable Tree of France in 2000. Its age is given as at least 400 years, and no source pushes the figure further, so that is where it stays.

The crown goes up about 20 metres. The species is Tilia cordata, the small-leaved lime: heart-shaped leaves, and a flush of scented flower in early summer that the bees find before you do.

The commune built a walking loop around it, the Boucle du tilleul et de la pierre à cupules, which takes in the tree and a prehistoric cup-marked stone in one afternoon. That is the honest measure of this one. It is a hamlet's own landmark in a corner of Haute-Savoie people already come to walk in, rather than a tree you cross the country for. No gate and no ticket, and no bus either: the last stretch is road from Féternes, then your feet.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 10.2 metres round at chest height, under a crown about 20 metres up. It stands on the square beside the thirteenth-century Chapelle de Château-Vieux, and the walking loop is signposted to it.

name: Tilleul de Grange Sauvaget
age_estimate: disputed: legend says about 550 years, one arborist's measurement suggests closer to 250

location.address: Lieu-dit Grange Sauvaget, hiking trail toward the Arloz farmstead, 39110 Bracon/Ivory, Jura
location.neighbourhood: Grange Sauvaget hamlet, between the villages of Bracon and Ivory

access: Free, on a public hiking trail (chemin de randonnée) between Bracon and the Arloz farmstead, with a picnic area and parking nearby per jura-tourism.com. A protective barrier rings the trunk itself (visible in krapooarboricole's photos) to stop visitors compacting the roots or climbing it, but the tree is otherwise openly viewable and the site is set up for visitors.
transport: Rural, no rail or bus stop; reached on foot via the signposted trail from Bracon or by car to the trailhead parking near Ivory/Bracon.
story:
Depending on who measured it, this lime is either 17 metres round and the largest in France, or 13.2 metres and merely enormous.

The 17 metre figure sits on tourist pages and appears to trace back to a measurement around 2003. In August 2009 a specialist put a tape around the trunk himself and got 13.2 metres at chest height, 12.9 lower down, and published the discrepancy rather than quietly picking a side. He could not say whether the gap is method or whether the tree has genuinely lost girth, since older photographs do show a fatter trunk. So 13.2 is the figure here, and the largest-in-France billing stays a billing.

The age runs the same way. Local tradition has it planted in 1477 for the marriage of Marie of Burgundy, daughter of Charles the Bold, to Maximilian of Habsburg, which would make it about 550. The same 2009 visit read the trunk dendrologically and came out at no more than 250. Three centuries of disagreement over one tree, unresolved.

What nobody argues about: it was declared of public utility in 1996, a barrier rings the trunk to keep feet off its roots, and when an autumn storm took a large limb in 2019 the commune of Bracon launched a campaign to save it that reached regional television. The trail out from Bracon has parking at one end and a picnic table at the tree.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the barrier ringing the trunk, put there to keep feet off the roots, and by the size of what it encloses, over 13 metres round. It stands on the trail between Bracon and the Arloz farmstead.

name: Tilleul de Réaumont

location.address: Behind the Église Saint-Jean-Baptiste, village centre, 38480 Réaumont, Isère

access: Free. Stands in the open village square/churchyard behind the Église Saint-Jean-Baptiste in the centre of Réaumont, with a dedicated grassed and protected area around it (the local road was rerouted to give it room, per krapooarboricole). Reachable by train from Grenoble in about 25 minutes to the Réaumont Saint-Cassien halt, then a short walk on foot through fields to the village square (per merveillescachees.com, 2020).
transport: Réaumont Saint-Cassien station (SNCF TER, Saint-Andre-le-Gaz line), about 25 minutes from Grenoble, then roughly a 10-15 minute walk on a path through fields to the village centre.
story:
In 1891 somebody filled this tree with masonry. In 2000 somebody else dug it all back out.

The trunk is entirely hollow, which is ordinary for a lime this old and was once thought to need fixing. It now stands on its own, held by metal bolts with a prop under one heavy limb, and it measures about 9.2 metres round. Visits between 2010 and 2017 came back with 9.05, 9.20 and 9.36, because a hollow, buttressed trunk does not measure the same way twice.

It is reckoned the oldest known tree in the Isère, planted around 1390, which makes it roughly 620 years old. Independent sources across a decade give the same figure, which is unusually consistent for a tree dated by tradition rather than by a core sample.

Réaumont has organised itself around it. The road was rerouted to give the tree room. A local association, La Maison de l'Arbre, was founded in 2001, and the village has run a tree festival twice a year since 1995. In 2013 it was shortlisted for France's Arbre de l'Année. In July 2020 a visitor described the crown as particularly well furnished with leaves, hollow trunk notwithstanding.

Twenty-five minutes on the train from Grenoble puts you at the Réaumont Saint-Cassien halt, and a path across the fields does the last of it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ironwork: metal bolts through the trunk and a prop under one heavy limb, on a hollow trunk 9.2 metres round. It stands on its own grassed ground behind the Église Saint-Jean-Baptiste.

best_time.label: late June, when the whole crown comes into scented flower

name: Cèdre pleureur de la Vallée-aux-Loups
species: Blue Weeping Atlas Cedar (Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca Pendula')

location.address: Domaine départemental de la Vallée-aux-Loups (Arboretum), 87-102 Rue de Chateaubriand, 92290 Châtenay-Malabry, Hauts-de-Seine
location.neighbourhood: Arboretum de la Vallée-aux-Loups, adjoining the Maison de Chateaubriand

access: Free. The arboretum and the wider Domaine départemental de la Vallée-aux-Loups (Arboretum, Île Verte, wooded park, Jardin de l'Aigle Blanc) are open to the public at no charge, per the Hauts-de-Seine department's own tourism pages and multiple independent visitor guides (only the adjoining Maison de Chateaubriand house tour charges separately, a few euros). Note: the English Wikipedia article on the arboretum states 'an admission fee is charged', which conflicts with every French-language official and tourism source found; treated as likely stale or referring only to the house, but flagged for a check before publishing.
transport: Tram T10 stops directly at 'Vallée aux Loups' in Châtenay-Malabry. Alternatively RER B to Robinson station, then bus 194 (Marc Sangnier or Lycée de Châtenay-Malabry stops) or a 20-25 minute signposted walk.
story:
Every blue weeping Atlas cedar in the world came off this one tree. The cultivar Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca Pendula' appeared here as a mutation around 1873, and every specimen since has been a cutting or a graft descended from it. If you have seen one draped over a lawn in a park or a garden somewhere, you have seen a copy of this.

It is about 150 years old, roughly five metres round and only 14 metres tall, and it spreads its branches across about 700 square metres, near enough a tennis court. The department calls it the largest of its kind anywhere, which more or less follows from being the first.

Weeping branches that long cannot hold themselves up. In 2011 the artist Francis Ballu made around thirty resin supports shaped like stalagmites and set them under the limbs, so the thing holding the tree together looks like a cave floor and visitors can still walk in underneath the canopy.

Who raised the original mutation is not quite settled. The department and Wikipedia credit the nurseryman Gustave Croux; some garden histories point instead to the Paillet nurseries in the same corner of Châtenay-Malabry. Both were in the business here in the same decades, and nobody has untangled it.

It won France's national tree prize in 2015. The arboretum is free, and the T10 tram stops at Vallée aux Loups.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the props: about thirty resin supports shaped like stalagmites, holding up branches that sweep the ground across an area the size of a tennis court. It is the tree you can walk in underneath.
